frictionVectors.title: European energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains an important market for Algerian gas, creating bargaining power but also exposure to pricing pressure and infrastructure dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: State dominance protects resource sovereignty, while dependence on oil and gas revenues constrains diversification and fiscal resilience.

frictionVectors.title: External control of logistics
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor attracts major Western and Gulf interest because of its strategic route toward Copperbelt minerals, raising questions over local value capture and long-term infrastructure concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Angola retains formal control over hydrocarbons but remains vulnerable to foreign operators, financing conditions, and volatile crude prices.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Cotonou and northbound trade corridors remain exposed to regional political disputes and external commercial influence, particularly involving Niger and Nigeria.

frictionVectors.title: Northern insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity near the Burkina Faso and Niger borders diverts state resources and threatens agricultural, mining, and transport infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-market exposure
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has secured substantial influence over diamond sorting and beneficiation, but remains exposed to global demand shifts and competition from lab-grown stones.

frictionVectors.title: Water and energy constraints
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported electricity and scarce water limits industrial autonomy and complicates efforts to expand domestic mineral processing.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The authorities are seeking greater state participation and local processing in gold mining, but this risks reducing investment and intensifying disputes with foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Security and external alignment
frictionVectors.details: Persistent insurgency threatens mines and transport routes, while deeper security ties with Russia and reduced Western engagement create new dependencies rather than full autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and Rare-Earth Informality
frictionVectors.details: Informal gold and coltan networks, including routes through neighboring states, limit government capture of resource revenues and create openings for foreign intermediaries.

frictionVectors.title: DRC Border and Aid Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Cross-border insecurity and Burundi's reliance on external finance constrain policy autonomy, while regional partners compete for influence over transport and mineral corridors.

frictionVectors.title: External Control of Strategic Ports
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, airport, and logistics investment strengthens connectivity but leaves critical infrastructure and maritime services exposed to external commercial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Tourism Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on tourism, remittances, and imported energy limits economic sovereignty during external shocks, particularly those affecting European markets.

frictionVectors.title: Resource Concessions and External Firms
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, timber, and mining concessions remain heavily shaped by foreign companies and opaque domestic networks, limiting transparent public value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Kribi and Douala corridors are strategically important to Chinese, European, and regional interests, while insecurity in the Far North and Northwest threatens transport reliability.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and Diamond Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Security-linked foreign operators and informal networks compete for gold and diamond access, with weak state oversight and limited local benefit from extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and Territorial Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on foreign security support and vulnerable road corridors reduces Bangui's effective control outside major urban centers and increases exposure to neighboring conflicts.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Oil Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil revenues and export infrastructure remain central to state solvency, leaving Chad vulnerable to foreign operators, price shocks, and disputes over revenue management.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan and Sahel Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan war and regional armed-group activity strain border control and humanitarian capacity, while external security partners compete for influence over N'Djamena.

frictionVectors.title: France–Comoros Territorial Tension
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to contest French control of Mayotte, while migration enforcement and maritime jurisdiction keep relations strained.

frictionVectors.title: Limited Economic Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: The country remains heavily dependent on remittances, imported energy, and external development finance, leaving infrastructure priorities vulnerable to outside agendas.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Bargaining Imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt production attracts major Chinese and multinational capital, but weak contract enforcement and limited domestic processing constrain Kinshasa's ability to capture value.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-Linked Conflict Dynamics
frictionVectors.details: M23-related insecurity and regional competition around eastern trade corridors continue to threaten state control, mining governance, and transport infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led offshore oil production dominates export earnings and public finances, limiting diversification and increasing exposure to external price and investment cycles.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-Finance Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese participation in roads, ports, and construction strengthens connectivity but raises concerns over debt, procurement transparency, and long-term strategic leverage.

highlights: Abidjan emerges as a regional hub

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Value-Chain Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire retains limited influence over global cocoa pricing and processing despite efforts to expand domestic transformation and producer protections.

frictionVectors.title: External Security and Infrastructure Links
frictionVectors.details: French, European, Gulf, and Chinese actors compete for roles in ports, logistics, energy, and security, creating opportunities but also potential strategic dependency.

frictionVectors.title: Base Politics and Strategic Competition
frictionVectors.details: The presence of US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities generates substantial revenue but narrows Djibouti's room for maneuver amid Red Sea and Indo-Pacific rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed infrastructure and reliance on port services linked to Ethiopia provide leverage and revenue while exposing the state to debt, concession, and regional-trade risks.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large IMF, Gulf, and bilateral financing needs give outside partners influence over fiscal policy, state assets, and strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Canal Security
frictionVectors.details: Attacks and instability around the Red Sea have reduced Suez Canal revenues while increasing Egypt's security burden and dependence on external maritime coordination.

frictionVectors.title: Maturing Oil and Gas Fields
frictionVectors.details: Declining hydrocarbon output constrains state revenue and increases pressure to attract foreign operators and develop offshore gas projects on less favorable terms.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-Access Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and financing remain important to national infrastructure, creating long-term leverage over strategic assets and procurement.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Assab and Massawa remain strategically valuable, but competition involving Ethiopia, Gulf states, and neighboring Red Sea actors exposes Eritrea to pressure over access and alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal production relies heavily on foreign technical and financial partners, limiting domestic control over extraction and export value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Transit and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini depends heavily on South African transport corridors, electricity links, customs systems, and markets, constraining independent economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and Forestry Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Agricultural exports and forestry remain vulnerable to external price shifts, water stress, and buyer concentration, limiting the state's bargaining power over resource value.

frictionVectors.title: Debt Restructuring Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt negotiations with international creditors and dependence on multilateral support constrain fiscal autonomy and influence the sequencing of infrastructure and exchange-rate reforms.

frictionVectors.title: Nile and Regional Security
frictionVectors.details: The GERD strengthens Ethiopia's control over its energy strategy but continues to generate friction with Egypt and Sudan amid wider instability in the Horn of Africa.

highlights: Manganese and oil remain strategic anchors

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining-contract leverage
frictionVectors.details: The post-coup authorities are seeking greater state participation and local processing in manganese and other minerals, creating friction with established foreign operators and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependency
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors and logistics remain dependent on external capital and operators, limiting Libreville's ability to convert resource wealth into fully sovereign industrial capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing access
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing by foreign fleets continues to strain coastal resources and enforcement capacity, with local communities receiving limited value from depleted stocks.

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked economic exposure
frictionVectors.details: Trade, energy, transport, and security ties with Senegal provide essential connectivity but constrain Banjul's room for independent economic and infrastructure policy.

highlights: Debt and illegal mining constrain sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector external leakage
frictionVectors.details: Illegal mining and illicit gold flows weaken fiscal control, damage farmland and water systems, and expose the state to entrenched domestic and foreign trading networks.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Accra is pressing for greater processing and domestic participation in lithium, bauxite, and manganese projects while balancing investor demands and IMF-era fiscal constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project is controlled through large foreign-backed consortia and requires extensive rail and port infrastructure, leaving Guinea dependent on outside finance and technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite enclave economics
frictionVectors.details: Bauxite exports remain dominated by foreign operators, while the junta's contract reviews and demands for local processing increase tensions with Chinese and other international partners.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew-processing dependency
frictionVectors.details: Most cashew value is captured through external buyers and regional processors, leaving producers vulnerable to price shocks and limiting domestic industrial upgrading.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime and fisheries pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing access and weak maritime enforcement reduce state control over coastal resources, while instability heightens risks of illicit trafficking through ports and border zones.

frictionVectors.title: External financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and large Chinese and Western infrastructure obligations constrain Nairobi's policy space. Debt-service pressure is pushing Kenya to renegotiate projects and seek broader creditor support.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and the LAPSSET corridor remain exposed to competition from Tanzania and external commercial operators. Control over logistics infrastructure is increasingly tied to Gulf, Chinese, and Western capital.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands water dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project makes national revenue and infrastructure planning heavily dependent on South Africa. Construction delays, cost overruns, and cross-border governance limit Maseru's bargaining autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-controlled diamond sector
frictionVectors.details: Diamond production is dominated by foreign-backed operators and remains vulnerable to price cycles and labor disputes. Limited domestic processing reduces Lesotho's capture of resource value.

frictionVectors.title: Mining concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore exports and associated rail and port infrastructure remain structured around foreign concessionaires. Liberia gains royalties and employment but retains limited control over pricing, logistics, and downstream processing.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor bargaining
frictionVectors.details: The use and expansion of Buchanan and other export corridors create competition among foreign mining and infrastructure interests. Weak fiscal capacity limits Monrovia's ability to impose stronger local-content or beneficiation terms.

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of oil facilities
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to influence terminals, fields, and the National Oil Corporation's operating environment. Production can be disrupted by localized blockades and elite bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: External military and energy influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, regional states, and European actors retain significant security or energy interests in Libya. Their involvement complicates unified management of offshore assets, export routes, and national security infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mineral value chains
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects are largely organized around foreign capital, technology, and export markets. Madagascar captures jobs and taxes but has limited downstream processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Mining infrastructure and community conflict
frictionVectors.details: Large mining operations depend on dedicated roads, ports, and power arrangements that can bypass broader national infrastructure needs. Land access, environmental impacts, and unreliable electricity continue to generate local resistance.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt distress and reliance on IMF, World Bank, and bilateral creditors constrain policy autonomy. Fiscal reforms and import restrictions carry significant social and political costs.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining Expansion
frictionVectors.details: Uranium, rare-earth, and other mineral projects are being promoted to generate foreign exchange, but limited domestic processing capacity risks leaving Malawi dependent on externally financed and operated supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque Security-for-Resources Alignment
frictionVectors.details: The military government relies heavily on Russian security support while seeking greater state control over gold and mining revenues. The arrangement may reduce Western influence but increases opacity and dependence on a narrow external partner.

frictionVectors.title: Jihadist Pressure on Resource Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups continue to threaten transport routes, mining zones, and agricultural production. Insecurity raises operating costs and limits Bamako's practical control over resource-producing regions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Dependence in Offshore Gas
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers major revenue potential but remains dependent on foreign operators, technology, and export infrastructure. Revenue governance and local-content delivery will determine whether gas strengthens national sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Border and Maritime Security
frictionVectors.details: Mauritania is exposed to spillover from instability in Mali and to strategic competition around Atlantic ports and offshore assets. Nouakchott is therefore balancing European, Gulf, Chinese, and regional security relationships.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Indian Ocean Access
frictionVectors.details: The Chagos sovereignty process remains strategically important for Mauritius because of fishing rights, maritime jurisdiction, and access to surrounding resources. Implementation arrangements involving the United Kingdom and the United States remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: External Capital Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius benefits from diversified tourism, finance, manufacturing, and investment links, but its small market remains vulnerable to shifts in Indian, Chinese, Gulf, and European capital flows.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Contestation
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate, fisheries, ports, and renewable-energy projects in Western Sahara generate strategic leverage but remain contested by the Polisario Front and Algeria. Legal and diplomatic disputes can affect foreign investment and trade access.

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on Foreign Technology and Finance
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is strengthening control over phosphates, renewables, and industrial logistics, yet major infrastructure and green-hydrogen ambitions still require European, Gulf, Chinese, and multilateral capital and technology.

highlights: Cabo Delgado security remains the LNG gatekeeper
Foreign-led gas projects dominate fiscal expectations

frictionVectors.title: LNG Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: International operators and financiers retain decisive influence over project timing, security arrangements, and revenue flows. Any restart of major LNG construction remains vulnerable to insurgent attacks and local grievances.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Corridor
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent activity continues to threaten offshore facilities, transport links, and surrounding communities. External military and security support improves protection but deepens Maputo's dependence on outside actors.

highlights: Oil discoveries are reshaping national bargaining power
Green hydrogen plans test local-value ambitions

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Control
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies control the capital, technology, and operational expertise needed to develop offshore discoveries. Windfall expectations are increasing pressure for stronger state participation and transparent fiscal terms.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrogen Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed green-hydrogen projects could diversify the economy, but export-oriented infrastructure risks creating enclaves with limited domestic industrial spillovers. Water use, land access, and local ownership remain politically sensitive.

highlights: Junta asserts control over uranium and hydrocarbons
Isolation strains export routes and investment capacity

frictionVectors.title: Uranium Rebalancing
frictionVectors.details: Niamey is seeking greater control over uranium assets and reducing French commercial influence. The transition risks legal disputes, declining investment, and disruption to already fragile mining operations.

frictionVectors.title: Export Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil exports and imports depend on infrastructure crossing neighboring states, especially Benin-linked routes. Diplomatic tensions, sanctions exposure, and insecurity raise the cost of converting resource ownership into reliable state revenue.

highlights: Oil-sector reform meets persistent production insecurity

frictionVectors.title: Upstream Production Losses
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline theft, vandalism, crude theft, and aging infrastructure continue to weaken public capture of petroleum value. International operators retain substantial technical and financial leverage despite regulatory reforms.

frictionVectors.title: Refining and Import Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Domestic refining capacity is improving, but fuel supply remains exposed to foreign exchange constraints, shipping markets, and politically sensitive subsidy decisions. The expanding Dangote refinery strengthens national leverage while creating new market-power concerns.

highlights: Mineral-traceability diplomacy is under mounting pressure
Regional security influence outpaces resource depth

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Allegations that Rwanda benefits from mineral flows linked to armed groups in eastern DRC continue to drive sanctions pressure and diplomatic friction. Kigali rejects the allegations, while international scrutiny threatens access to premium, traceable supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Strategic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong administrative control but remains reliant on foreign aid, investment, and security partnerships. External pressure over regional military activity and governance increasingly constrains its room for maneuver.

highlights: Offshore oil remains a strategic prospect
Small-state diplomacy balances Europe, China and Gulf partners

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE EXPLORATION UNCERTAINTY
frictionVectors.details: Potential petroleum resources in the Gulf of Guinea attract outside operators, but commercial viability and regulatory capacity remain uncertain. Maritime boundary management with Nigeria also limits unilateral control.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The country relies heavily on external financing and technical assistance for ports, power and transport infrastructure, creating leverage for European, Chinese and Gulf partners.

highlights: Resource-sovereignty agenda meets first oil and gas revenues
Dakar is renegotiating the terms of external capital

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON CONTRACT RENEGOTIATION
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing for greater national participation and revised fiscal terms in offshore oil and gas projects, creating tension with international operators and lenders. Production has begun, but revenue governance and debt pressures remain unresolved.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE SECURITY AND FISHERIES
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fishing and maritime competition strain local livelihoods and enforcement capacity. Offshore energy infrastructure adds another layer of security and sovereignty concerns.

highlights: Blue-economy control is central to national sovereignty
Indian Ocean partnerships expand maritime capacity

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME INFLUENCE COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles uses partnerships with India, France and other external actors to patrol its extensive maritime zone, while Chinese engagement remains a strategic consideration. Dependence on outside capabilities can constrain autonomous security policy.

frictionVectors.title: TOURISM AND DEBT VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains highly exposed to foreign tourism, imported infrastructure and climate shocks. External financing and investment can support resilience while also limiting policy space over land, ports and coastal development.

highlights: Mineral wealth is expanding faster than domestic control
Rail, port and mining corridors shape strategic influence

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONCESSION DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile and other mineral projects depend heavily on foreign capital, technology and export infrastructure. The state is seeking more local value capture, but fiscal and bargaining power remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND LOGISTICS LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Mining-linked rail and port investments give external operators substantial influence over export routes and regional infrastructure. Weak domestic industrial capacity limits Sierra Leone's ability to move beyond raw-material exports.

highlights: Security dependence shadows emerging offshore energy ambitions
Turkey, Gulf states and neighbors compete for strategic access

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE OIL AND CONTRACT GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Federal and regional authorities are courting foreign oil companies while disputes over licensing, revenue sharing and constitutional jurisdiction remain unresolved. Weak security and regulatory capacity increase the risk that future resource gains will accrue disproportionately to external operators.

frictionVectors.title: PORT ACCESS AND REGIONAL RIVALRY
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf actors and neighboring states seek influence through ports, bases, security agreements and infrastructure projects. The Ethiopia-Somaliland dispute has intensified concerns over territorial sovereignty and control of maritime access.

highlights: Power and port bottlenecks constrain autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and grid dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eskom's aging fleet, transmission constraints, and reliance on private generation limit industrial sovereignty and raise pressure for external capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are competing for battery and platinum-group mineral access, while South Africa seeks greater domestic beneficiation.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-export corridor vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on pipelines and terminals in Sudan, leaving national revenue exposed to Sudan's war, sabotage risks, and external control of transit infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Regional mediation, foreign security assistance, and humanitarian financing remain essential as political elites contest power and resource access.

highlights: Gold and ports attract outside patrons

frictionVectors.title: Gold networks and wartime financing
frictionVectors.details: Competing armed actors and foreign-linked traders use gold production and export channels to finance the conflict, weakening civilian control over mineral wealth.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Port access and logistics assets on the Red Sea are strategically contested by regional and extra-regional powers, increasing leverage over Sudan's fragmented authorities.

highlights: LNG and corridor projects expand leverage

frictionVectors.title: LNG development and fiscal control
frictionVectors.details: Negotiations over liquefied natural gas aim to attract major investment while preserving state revenue, local-content requirements, and long-term control over gas assets.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and transport corridors
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed rail, port, and logistics projects can strengthen Tanzania's regional role but may create strategic dependence if concession terms and debt exposure are poorly managed.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional logistics hub

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics influence
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's deep-water port and associated corridors attract foreign operators and financing, creating growth opportunities alongside concerns over strategic infrastructure dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Northern spillover insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence and instability spreading from Burkina Faso threaten northern transport routes and may increase reliance on external security support.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: European migration cooperation and financial support give Brussels significant leverage over Tunisian policy. Debt constraints limit Tunis's bargaining room with external lenders and partners.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining domestic production and reliance on imported hydrocarbons expose Tunisia to price shocks and foreign supply conditions. Phosphate-sector weakness further reduces export leverage.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sanctions
frictionVectors.details: The oil pipeline remains central to Uganda's resource strategy but faces sustained environmental, human-rights, and financing pressure from Western governments and institutions. Chinese and other non-Western partners provide alternatives but increase long-term dependency risks.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security burden
frictionVectors.details: Uganda's military role in regional operations protects influence but imposes fiscal and political costs. Instability around eastern DRC and South Sudan threatens transport, trade, and future energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt attract intense investment from Chinese, Western, and Gulf-linked firms, creating opportunities for diversification but leaving Zambia exposed to external pricing and capital decisions. Efforts to expand local processing remain constrained by power and logistics gaps.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and corridor vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower shortages directly threaten mining output and industrial autonomy. Dependence on regional transport corridors and imported electricity gives neighboring states and infrastructure financiers additional leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-mineral dependency
frictionVectors.details: Lithium, platinum, and gold draw major Chinese and other foreign investment, while limited domestic processing keeps much of the value chain offshore. Export controls and beneficiation mandates improve state leverage but have not overcome financing and technology dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Debt, sanctions, and payment constraints
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions, arrears, and weak access to international finance restrict infrastructure investment and complicate sovereign economic management. Currency instability encourages reliance on external hard-currency channels and mineral revenues.
